messages.author: 6367030a31173e4d
messages.subject: RE: Spatial autocorrelation
parts:
Hello again,

 

I’m writing an update to my previous email found below regarding spatial autocorrelation. I’ve got my head round this now and will conduct a couple of tests to see if it is significant for my dataset. But my question is; does it actually matter if spatial autocorrelation exists when simply providing an overall density estimate of a survey area if there is no temporal autocorrelation? I can’t think why this would be an issue unless you are interested in splitting the area into blocks, investigating distribution or incorporating this estimate into certain types of model to predict a cause of impact for example. Please correct me if I am wrong!?

 

Many thanks again,

 

Gemma Veneruso

 




 

From: distance...@googlegroups.com [mailto:distance...@googlegroups.com] On Behalf Of Gemma Veneruso
Sent: 22 June 2016 17:55
To: eric.r...@st-andrews.ac.uk; distance...@googlegroups.com
Subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Calculated covered area looks incorrect

 

Dear Eric and mailing list,

 

A very belated thank you for your last reply Eric. It turns out that I had simply converted my area units incorrectly resulting in too small a density!

 

I have a separate query now. It has been mentioned to me that spatial autocorrelation could be an issue if not analysed appropriately. To remind you of my dataset, I have conducted around 12 months of (almost monthly) line-transect survey data at sea with a view of estimating harbour porpoise density. I designed a series of zig zag transect lines equally spaced from one another, each of which were chosen at random per survey. Each leg within a single transect was treated as an independent sample. Some lines have been surveyed more than once (months apart from each other). Between one and two transects were surveyed per day.

 

It has been suggested that spatial autocorrelation could be present and should be accounted for, perhaps because I have classified a sample as a survey leg. I’m struggling to get my head around this concept…If you have locations A, B and C in increasing distance from one another. Detection 1 is at A. If spatially correlated, detection 2 is most likely to occur at B compared to C due to the closer vicinity of A. Is this spatial autocorrelation??

 

If I look at a GIS plots of my data and think back to surveys, there are certain days were a lot more animals are seen in a short space of time (and space) than others. However, in reality most marine mammal datasets should see this since there will be some feature (spatial or temporal) that is attractive to an animal, and therefore other animals….I do not think that I see a trend of many detections on one leg resulting in a glut of detections on the next leg. Is this what I need to check? For info. each leg is around 5 km and takes about 30 mins to complete. There are certainly no concentrations of detections at the start and end of legs where the distance between these is the smallest. It is true that the encounter rate is highly variable depending on the day. However this has been balanced out temporally by ensuring almost even coverage of the temporal feature that I believe may drive porpoise distribution. But now I’m talking about temporal autocorrelation….I think…I’m confused!

 

Lastly Buckland et al 2001 p 130 states that the assumption of objects being detected and distributed independently is not a significant issue when estimating density.

 

If anyone could help relieve my confusion and advise on whether I have an issue here that would be much appreciated!

 

Many thanks again for your time,

 

Gemma

 

 



 

From: Eric Rexstad [mailto:er...@st-andrews.ac.uk]
Sent: 07 June 2016 15:03
To: Gemma Veneruso <g.ven...@bangor.ac.uk>; distance...@googlegroups.com
Subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Calculated covered area looks incorrect

 

Gemma

It is useful that you have performed a "sense check" on your analysis, and have concluded that all is not as it should be.

My suspicion is that the units in which you measured your perpendicular distances (m possibly?) is not the same as the units in which you measured effort (transect length, km perhaps).  Unfortunately I don't know the units in which you measured either of those things.

Start from what you do know.  You should know the size of your study area (and the units in which it was measured); is 136000 correct?  Your email suggests the study area is 136km^2, so 136000 does not correspond to that either in km or in m.  The covered area of 487871514 divided by the effort (609839.4) *does* correspond to a truncation distance (w) of 400 (strip width=2w) as the output shows.

You can work back through your effort and perpendicular measurements and study area units to discern what has been entered improperly.  Read through the help regarding the argument "convert.units" in the function ds(); specifically the section of help entitled "Units" regarding that function.

 

On 03/06/2016 11:53, Gemma Veneruso wrote:

Hello,

 

I am conducting a CDS analysis using R on harbour porpoise line-transect data. My query relates to the calculated covered area which is very high compared to the total study area (A) and therefore looks wrong. As a result I am getting very low density, abundance and encounter rates. See figures below:

Abundance:

  Label   Estimate          se        cv        lcl        ucl       df

1 Total 0.02842298 0.005977053 0.2102895 0.01878345 0.04300945 76.95691

 

Density:

  Label     Estimate           se        cv          lcl          ucl       df

1 Total 2.089925e-07 4.394892e-08 0.2102895 1.381136e-07 3.162459e-07 76.95691

 

 

Around half of the transects were surveyed twice but this still doesn’t explain the high covered area relative to total area. As I understand it the covered area should be 2wL (or is it 2wLPa?). If using the truncation value of 400m the calculation (2wL) seems almost correct at   487871520 m2 (but not quite, haven’t worked out how the figure presented was calculated). However, the Distance examples at www.distancesampling.org/R  show outputs of covered area equal to survey area. Further to this, an estimate of 101 animals in a 136km2 area should surely not equate to such a low encounter rate and density value. Can you advise as to what has gone wrong here or if I am interpreting this incorrectly? The only thing I can think is wrong is the total length surveyed (L). I’ve looked over it and the length of each transect seems about right. Being on a vessel in strong currents, there is some variation in completed transect lengths compared to the pre-determined tracks and I have used the actual distance travelled. Perhaps this is a separate question, but would I be better to use the equal values of the pre-determined tracks?

 

Many thanks,

 

Gemma Veneruso

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] RE: Spatial autocorrelation
parts:
Hi Gemma, hi listfolk,

I think this question is hard to answer in general and depends at least
a little on the model that you fitted and your inferential goal.

There probably is spatial autocorrelation along your transects, but you
may be already modelling that via either a smooth of space or other
terms in your model that vary at the same scale (e.g. what appears to be
autocorrelation may be down to prey patches, which you might be able to
model via some covariate, like primary productivity or just a smooth of
space). In some sense we are interested in the autocorrelation
conditional on the model that has been fitted -- the residual
autocorrelation. Models with smooths of space in them may be already
taking this into account, provided they can be flexible enough.

So, you may not need to worry about this. Using a correllogram or
plotting box plots of the residuals by spatial area may be an easy way
to address this (see, e.g. Marra, Miller and Zanin (2011)).


Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave


Marra, G., Miller, D. L., & Zanin, L. (2011). Modelling the
spatiotemporal distribution of the incidence of resident foreign
population. Statistica Neerlandica, 66(2), 133–160.
http://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9574.2011.00500.x
